chapters.title: Chapter 6: Financing Working Capital in India

lessons.title: Receivables Financing and Supply Chain Finance: Factoring, Invoice Discounting and TReDS

children.text: Chapter 4 treated receivables as something to collect. This lesson treats them as something to sell. A confirmed invoice on a creditworthy buyer is an asset with a market, and in India that market has become genuinely accessible in the last few years.

The core idea is simple and powerful: if your buyer is more creditworthy than you, financing arranged on the buyer's name costs less than borrowing on your own. That gap is the whole business model behind everything in this lesson.
Four Ways to Turn an Invoice Into Cash

children.text: The distinction that matters most is

. A financing arrangement with recourse looks like a sale but behaves like a loan: if the buyer does not pay, you repay the financier, the receivable never really left your balance sheet, and your exposure is unchanged. Without recourse, the credit risk genuinely transfers.

markDefs.definition: A financing arrangement where the seller must repay the financier if the buyer fails to pay, so the risk never actually leaves the seller.

children.text: is the most important development for Indian small suppliers in the last decade. Several RBI-licensed platforms operate, including RXIL, M1xchange, Invoicemart and C2treds. The mechanism is an auction.

markDefs.definition: Trade Receivables Discounting System. RBI-licensed electronic platforms where invoices on large buyers are auctioned to financiers.

body.title: One invoice through a TReDS platform

events.title: Supplier uploads the invoice
events.description: The supplier, a registered micro, small or medium enterprise, uploads an invoice raised on a registered large buyer.

events.title: Buyer accepts
events.description: The buyer confirms the invoice on the platform. This acceptance is what converts a disputed-in-principle receivable into a financeable asset, and it is the step that makes the buyer's credit the relevant risk.

events.title: Financiers bid
events.description: Banks and non-bank financiers bid discount rates in an auction. The supplier sees competing rates rather than accepting whatever its own bank offers.

events.title: Supplier is paid
events.description: The winning financier pays the supplier the invoice value less the discount, typically without recourse.

events.title: Buyer pays the financier
events.description: The buyer settles the full invoice amount with the financier on the original due date. Nothing about the buyer's payment timing has changed.

body.caption: The cost of getting paid now instead of on the due date

children.text: Take a ₹2 crore invoice with 60 days to run. The supplier's own cash credit costs 11.5%, so waiting out the 60 days ties up funding worth about ₹3,78,082. If the auction discovers a rate of 8.5% because the financier is taking the large buyer's risk rather than the supplier's, the discount is about ₹2,79,452. The supplier saves roughly ₹0.99 lakh and gets the cash in two or three days instead of sixty.

body.title: Cost of funding one ₹2 crore invoice for 60 days (₹)

body.text: The third bar is the one most small suppliers actually choose. Funding the wait by delaying their own suppliers looks free, but Chapter 5 showed what forfeited discounts and statutory MSME interest really cost. Priced honestly, it is the most expensive option on the chart.

body.label: What financing does to the cycle
body.context: A supplier with ₹24 crore of sales cutting days sales outstanding from 65 to 30 by financing part of its book frees about ₹2.3 crore of working capital permanently.

body.title: Price a discounting transaction
body.prompt: A supplier discounts an ₹80 lakh invoice with 75 days left to the due date, at a discount rate of 9.2% a year. What is the discount charge, in rupees?
body.explanation: The charge is ₹80,00,000 times 9.2%, times 75 divided by 365, which is about ₹1,51,233. Compare that with what the supplier pays on its own borrowing for the same 75 days before deciding, and remember the transaction is usually without recourse, which has value beyond the rate.

children.text: Who Must Be on the Platform

TReDS works only if large buyers participate, so participation was made compulsory. A Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises notification dated 7 November 2024 requires every company under the Companies Act, 2013 with annual turnover above ₹250 crore, and all central public sector enterprises, to register on a TReDS platform. That superseded the 2018 notification, which had set the threshold at ₹500 crore, and brought several thousand more companies onto the platforms.

body.text: If your company crosses ₹250 crore of turnover, registration is a compliance obligation, not a financing choice. Registering is also not the same as accepting invoices promptly: a buyer that registers and then delays acceptance leaves suppliers unable to discount, which defeats the purpose and keeps the MSME interest clock from Chapter 5 running.

body.title: The same platform, two very different motivations

columns.label: For the supplier
points: Cash in two or three days instead of 45 or 60
A rate discovered by auction, based on the buyer's credit rather than your own
Usually without recourse, so the receivable genuinely leaves the balance sheet
No collateral and no drawing power calculation involved
Days sales outstanding falls, which improves every ratio a lender looks at

columns.label: For the buyer
points: Suppliers get paid early without the buyer paying early
Compliance with the registration mandate above ₹250 crore of turnover
A cleaner answer to the MSME 45-day problem than a March payment sweep
Room to negotiate better prices, since certainty of early payment is worth something to the supplier
In reverse factoring structures, the buyer can extend its own terms while the supplier is paid sooner

children.text: , and it is where large Indian buyers now do most of their supply chain finance. The buyer arranges a programme with a bank, approves invoices, and the bank pays suppliers early at a rate reflecting the buyer's rating. The supplier improves its cycle, the buyer often extends its own payment terms, and the bank is comfortable because it is taking a large corporate's risk. Everyone gains, provided the structure is disclosed honestly.

markDefs.definition: Reverse factoring. Financing arranged around the buyer's credit rating and approval, so the supplier is paid early at the buyer's cost of funds rather than its own.

children.text: The legal framework. Factoring in India is governed by the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, which was amended in 2021 to widen the range of non-bank financiers permitted to undertake factoring and to require assignments to be registered with the Central Registry. The amendment was aimed squarely at increasing the flow of receivables finance to smaller businesses, and the growth of the TReDS platforms since then reflects that.

Accounting treatment. Whether the receivable leaves your balance sheet depends on whether the risks and rewards genuinely transfer. A without-recourse sale derecognises the receivable, which is what improves days sales outstanding. A with-recourse arrangement keeps the receivable on the books and shows the advance as borrowing, so it funds the business without flattering any ratio.

Reverse factoring and disclosure. Because reverse factoring lets a buyer stretch payment terms while suppliers are paid early, a large programme can make a buyer's payables look like ordinary trade credit when they are closer to bank borrowing. Analysts have become alert to this, and disclosure expectations have tightened internationally. If you are analysing a company with rapidly rising payable days, check whether a supply chain finance programme explains it, exactly as Chapter 2 taught you to question any sharp move in payable days.

body.title: Why is the TReDS rate lower?
body.question: A small auto component supplier borrows at 11.5% on its cash credit limit, but discounts invoices on a TReDS platform at 8.5%. Why is the platform rate lower?
options: Because TReDS is subsidised by the government
Because once the buyer accepts the invoice, the financier is taking the large buyer's credit risk rather than the supplier's
Because the tenor is shorter than a cash credit limit
Because the supplier pledges more security on the platform
body.explanation: Acceptance by the buyer is the pivot. After it, the financier expects payment from a large, well-rated buyer, so it prices the buyer's risk. No security is pledged and no subsidy is involved: the saving comes entirely from whose credit is being assessed.

body.title: The word that decides everything
body.textWithBlank: A financing arrangement made with ___ leaves the credit risk with the seller, so the receivable stays on the balance sheet and behaves like a loan rather than a sale.
body.explanation: With recourse, the seller must repay the financier if the buyer does not pay. Without recourse, the risk and the receivable both transfer, which is why TReDS transactions improve days sales outstanding while with-recourse discounting does not.

body.title: Two offers on the same receivable book
body.scenario: You run finance at a ₹40 crore turnover auto component maker. Sixty per cent of your sales go to two large listed original equipment manufacturers on 60-day terms, and your cash credit limit of ₹8 crore is fully drawn at 11.5%. Your bank offers to raise the limit by ₹3 crore against additional collateral from the promoter. Separately, both your large customers are registered on a TReDS platform, where your invoices are currently being bid at around 8.6%.
body.prompt: Which route would you take, and what would you watch?
body.modelAnswer:
Take the TReDS route first, and treat the limit enhancement as a second, smaller conversation.

The arithmetic is decisive. Sixty per cent of ₹40 crore is ₹24 crore of annual sales to those two buyers, and on 60-day terms roughly ₹3.9 crore of receivables is outstanding from them at any time. Discounting that at 8.6% instead of funding it at 11.5% saves about 2.9 percentage points, and more importantly it does not need collateral from the promoter, a personal guarantee, or a drawing power calculation that shrinks in a bad month.

There is a second gain that matters more than the rate. Without-recourse discounting takes those receivables off your balance sheet, so your days sales outstanding falls sharply, your current ratio improves and your next limit renewal is a much easier conversation. You are also no longer carrying two-customer concentration risk on your own book.

What to watch. First, acceptance discipline: the mechanism only works if the buyers accept invoices promptly, so track acceptance lag per buyer and escalate it commercially, not just operationally. Second, rate volatility: auction rates move with liquidity, so do not model 8.6% as permanent. Third, the 40% of sales going to smaller customers, which TReDS does not reach, still needs the cash credit limit, so ask for a smaller enhancement rather than none. Fourth, and most important, do not let the released cash simply fund longer credit to the remaining customers. Financing improves the funding of the cycle. It does not shorten the cycle, and the two are easy to confuse.

body.title: Use receivables finance without fooling yourself
steps: Check whether your major customers are registered on a TReDS platform, and ask them to register if their turnover exceeds ₹250 crore.
Compare the auction rate against your own marginal cost of borrowing, not against your average cost.
Establish whether each arrangement is with or without recourse, since that decides both the risk and the accounting.
Track buyer acceptance lag on the platform, because an unaccepted invoice cannot be financed.
Model the working capital released, and decide in advance what it will be used for.
Do not treat financing as a substitute for collections discipline on the rest of the book.
If you are the buyer, check whether a reverse factoring programme would solve your MSME payment obligations more cleanly than a March payment sweep.
If you are analysing a company, check whether rising payable days are explained by a supply chain finance programme rather than by negotiating strength.

body.label: Receivables Exchange of India (RXIL)
body.description: One of the RBI-licensed TReDS platforms. The registration requirements and process pages are the fastest way to see what participation actually involves for a supplier, a buyer or a financier.

body.text: Financing a receivable does not shorten your cycle by a single day. It changes who funds the cycle and at what price. Both are worth improving, but do not mistake one for the other.

points: A confirmed invoice on a creditworthy buyer can be sold, and when the buyer is stronger than the seller, the financing costs less than the seller's own borrowing.
Whether an arrangement is with or without recourse decides both where the credit risk sits and whether the receivable leaves the balance sheet.
TReDS platforms auction accepted invoices to competing financiers, with the supplier typically paid within two or three days and without recourse.

Companies with turnover above ₹250 crore and all central public sector enterprises must register on a TReDS platform, under the notification of 7 November 2024 that replaced the earlier ₹500 crore threshold.
Reverse factoring lets a buyer pay suppliers early at its own cost of funds, and is a cleaner answer to the MSME payment rule than a year-end payment sweep.
A large reverse factoring programme can make bank funding look like trade payables, so rising payable days deserve that question.
Receivables finance changes who funds the cycle, not how long the cycle is.
